verses.translation_literal: A Maskil, of Ethan the Ezrahite.
verses.translation_dramatic: A song to make the hearer wise, set down in the name of Ethan, the Ezrahite.
verses.directors_commentary:
This line is not part of the song; it is the label on the scroll, and in the Hebrew text it is verse 1. That is why the KJV numbers the first line of the psalm itself as 89:1, one verse behind the Hebrew. Treat it as a spoken heading, plain and a little formal, the way a cantor names the piece before the first note.

'Maskil' comes from a root meaning to act with insight, and it heads thirteen psalms. Whether it names a kind of poem, a style of performance or a teaching piece is not settled; the KJV simply leaves the word untranslated, as 'Maschil', which is honest. 'Of Ethan' can mean 'by' Ethan, 'for' him or 'in his collection'. The Ezrahite is a wise man in 1 Kings 5:11 (English 4:31), set beside Solomon as someone Solomon outshone. Radak and Meiri take him for that man, a descendant of Zerah son of Judah, and so a voice from Israel's own circle of sages. The rabbis read him instead as Abraham, 'raised up from the east' (Isaiah 41:2), a reading Rashi reports. Pitch the actor's voice as one who has both wisdom and a grievance, because the psalm goes on to turn from praise to complaint.

philological_notes.note: A heading term from the root 'to have insight, to act wisely'. Its exact meaning as a genre or musical label is disputed; Meiri takes it as a song that stirs the heart to understanding.
'The Ezrahite', a family name usually linked to Zerah, son of Judah. Radak holds this Ethan is the sage of 1 Kings 5:11 (English 4:31); the rabbis read the word as 'from the east', of Abraham.

verses.translation_literal: The loyal acts of YHWH for ever I will sing; to generation and generation I will make known your faithfulness with my mouth.
verses.translation_dramatic: The LORD's loyal love: that is my song, and I will sing it without end. From one generation to the next my own mouth will carry your faithfulness, and I will tell it, and tell it again.
verses.directors_commentary: The speaker opens with a vow, and it is a public one: 'with my mouth' means the actor is telling people, not musing to himself. Speak the first line as a settled promise, steady and warm; this warmth is what the rest of the psalm will break against. 'Chasdei' is covenant loyalty, the obligation a stronger party freely takes on toward a weaker one, which is why 'mercies' (KJV) is too soft: it sounds like pity, whereas the word means a bond that is kept. 'Emunah' is steadiness, what holds under weight. The two words come back more than a dozen times in the psalm and the whole poem is a quarrel over whether both still hold. 'Le-dor va-dor', 'to generation and generation', is the ancient idiom for 'always', and the KJV's 'to all generations' flattens the repeated word into a quantity.

philological_notes.note: Plural of chesed, loyalty owed within a covenant relationship; the plural points to its repeated acts. 'Mercies' (KJV) is only one part of the sense.
From the root 'to be firm, to support'. It means reliability, being as good as one's word, rather than 'faith' in the modern sense.

verses.translation_literal: For I have said: for ever loyalty will be built; the heavens, you establish your faithfulness in them.
verses.translation_dramatic: For I have said it, and I believed it: love will be built to last for ever, a thing raised stone on stone. And you set your faithfulness in the heavens themselves, as fixed as they are.
verses.directors_commentary: 'For I have said' is a quotation of the speaker's own earlier conviction, and a careful actor will hear in the past tense a hint that the conviction is under strain. The image is architectural: loyalty is 'built' (yibaneh) and faithfulness is 'established' (takhin) in the sky, the one thing no ancient person ever saw fall. The point is that God's word is as dependable as the vault of heaven. The KJV smooths this into 'in the very heavens', adding 'very' and turning a flat statement into an emphasis the Hebrew does not mark. The verb 'build' is the same root that will return in verse 5 for the throne, and the hearer is meant to connect the two: the house of David is part of the structure.

philological_notes.note: 'Will be built' (niphal). The root recurs in verse 5 for building David's throne, and a Davidic 'house' is a pun in 2 Samuel 7 on 'build'.
'You establish', hiphil of the root meaning 'to be firm'. The same verb is used in verse 5 as 'I will establish' (akhin), so God's verb for the heavens becomes his verb for the dynasty.

verses.translation_literal: I have cut a covenant for my chosen one; I have sworn to David my servant:
verses.translation_dramatic: I have cut a covenant with the one I chose. I have sworn it, and I swore it to David, my servant.
verses.directors_commentary:
The poet now steps aside and God speaks. Everything up to here was 'I will sing'; from here the voice is the LORD's own, quoting the promise on which the whole psalm rests. Give it the weight of a legal deposition, short clauses, no hurry.

The verb is 'cut' a covenant. In the ancient Near East a treaty was sealed by cutting animals in two and walking between the pieces (Genesis 15:9-18; Jeremiah 34:18-19), so the idiom carries the image of a binding that cost blood. The KJV's 'made a covenant' is accurate but flattens the picture. A second, weightier act follows: 'I have sworn'. The verb is passive in form (Niphal) and means to bind oneself by an oath; a covenant stated and then sworn by God is as secure as an ancient king's word could be. Radak hears in the oath that its words stand for ever.

Two titles for David carry the politics. 'My chosen one' says the kingship comes by divine choice, not inheritance or conquest; it was Israel's answer to the claims of neighbouring kings who ruled by the favour of Baal, Marduk or Amun. 'My servant' is not demeaning: in royal courts it is the title of the most trusted official, and for a king under God it names the office. The KJV's 'with my chosen' glosses the preposition 'for' and drops the sense of benefit; the Hebrew says 'for my chosen one'. The Targum has Abraham here, reading the chosen one as the patriarch, a late interpretive turn the Hebrew does not require. The verse ends with a colon-like pause, because the next verse gives the content of the oath: your seed for ever.

philological_notes.note: Literally 'I have cut a covenant', the standard idiom for making a treaty, from the rite of cutting animals. The 'cut' stays visible in the literal layer.
Niphal of the verb 'to swear': to bind oneself by an oath. God swears here, so the promise is doubly guaranteed, covenant plus oath. Radak adds only that the words of this oath stand for ever.
'My servant': in royal usage a title of honour for the trusted agent of a ruler, applied to David as the king under God.

verses.translation_literal: Until perpetuity I will establish your seed, and I will build to generation and generation your throne. Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: As long as time itself runs, I will make your line stand. And from age to age, I will build your throne. Selah.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the oath itself, and it is the hinge of the whole psalm, so the actor must give it full weight; a listener has to remember exactly what was promised. Two promises, in parallel: the 'seed' (zera', offspring) will be established, and the throne will be built, generation after generation. 'Until perpetuity' (ad olam) is an enormous claim, but also an ordinary idiom for 'as far as the eye can see'; the later anguish depends on how literally it was taken. The KJV 'build up' adds a direction the Hebrew lacks. 'Selah' is a marker whose meaning is lost, perhaps a pause, perhaps a raising of voices or instruments. Leave a beat. Silence is the safest reading.

philological_notes.note: A liturgical marker whose meaning is uncertain: a pause, an instrumental interlude, or a lifting of voices. It is left untranslated.

verses.translation_literal: And the heavens will praise your wonder, YHWH, also your faithfulness in the assembly of holy ones.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let the heavens themselves give thanks for the wonder you do, O LORD, and let your faithfulness be sung in the gathering of the holy ones.
verses.directors_commentary: The speaker turns from the oath back to praise, and the scene lifts into the sky: this is the first hint of a heavenly court. 'Pele', 'wonder', is the word for acts beyond human power, here used in the singular as a quality of God. 'The assembly of holy ones' (qehal qedoshim) is the company of divine beings around God's throne, which Rashi, Radak and Ibn Ezra read as angels; the KJV's 'saints' makes an audience think of devout humans, which is a later sense. The Hebrew places YHWH's faithfulness before witnesses who cannot be bribed or fooled, so his word is guaranteed by the court of heaven. That sets up the rhetorical question of verse 7.

philological_notes.note: 'Holy ones', set-apart beings. In this context the members of the heavenly court, as the commentators take them, rather than human 'saints' (KJV).
'Your wonder', the extraordinary deed that exceeds ordinary power; singular, as a collective for the whole of his marvels.

verses.translation_literal: For who in the cloud-sky can be set beside YHWH? Who is like YHWH among the sons of gods?
verses.translation_dramatic: For who in the clouds above can stand beside the LORD? Who among the sons of the gods is anything like him?
verses.directors_commentary: A rhetorical question: the expected answer is 'no one', and the actor should let the silence after it answer. In its world this is a daring claim, because the neighbours of Israel counted a real company of gods above. 'Bene elim', literally 'sons of gods', is the standard term for a divine council, the lesser beings who surround the high god in Canaanite texts. The psalm does not deny that they exist; it denies that any of them is comparable. That is polemic against the sky-gods of the surrounding peoples, told as a courtroom of wonder. The KJV's 'the sons of the mighty' turns the gods into 'the strong', which hides the polemic; 'in the heaven' is also looser than 'shachaq', the thin cloud-layer, the dust of the skies. The wordplay is in the verbs: 'ya'aroch' (be set in order beside, rank with) and 'yidmeh' (be like) say the same thing twice, once about status and once about likeness.

philological_notes.note: 'Among the sons of gods', the members of the divine council. Medieval commentators read angels or stars; the plain sense is the heavenly court, whose members are non-comparable to YHWH.
'To be set in order alongside, ranked with'; a verb of comparison of worth, paired with 'yidmeh' (is like), which is comparison of likeness.

verses.translation_literal: God, feared in the council of the holy ones, great, and awesome above all around him.
verses.translation_dramatic: God: dreaded in the inner circle of the holy ones, vast in his majesty, and more fearsome than all who stand around him.
verses.directors_commentary: From question to portrait. 'Sod' is the secret deliberation of a council, the room where decisions are made, not a public 'assembly' as the KJV has it; the audience should picture the inner chamber of heaven, and God's holy ones afraid in it. In the Near East, a king was measured by the awe of his courtiers. Here the courtiers themselves tremble. 'Na'arats', 'feared', is a rare, strong verb for dread, close to the trembling of a person before an overpowering force. The KJV 'greatly to be feared' takes 'rabbah' as an adverb; I take it as describing the council, 'great', which also fits Meiri's reading. The last phrase, 'all around him', is the throne-room image of attendants standing in a ring.

philological_notes.note: A council in session, an intimate circle of counsel; elsewhere (Jer 23:18) the place where a prophet is said to stand and hear the divine word. 'Assembly' (KJV) loses the sense of secret deliberation.
'Feared, dreaded', a rare verb of trembling awe, stronger than ordinary respect.

verses.translation_literal: YHWH, God of hosts, who is like you, mighty Yah? And your faithfulness is around you.
verses.translation_dramatic: O LORD, God of the armies of heaven, who is like you, mighty Yah? And all around you stands your faithfulness, like a wall of guards.
verses.directors_commentary: The speaker now addresses God directly, in a cry. Open with a full title: YHWH, God of hosts, the divine warrior who leads heaven's armies. That title belongs to Israel's holy-war tradition, and it makes the question 'who is like you?' sound like a battle shout. 'Chasin', 'mighty', occurs only here in the Bible and so the KJV's 'a strong Lord' guesses. It belongs to a family with 'chason' (strong, as the oaks of Amos 2:9), as Ibn Ezra, Meiri and Metzudat Zion note. 'Yah' is the short form of the divine name, used in strong praise. Notice the last clause: 'faithfulness' is not something God has, it is something that surrounds him, as a bodyguard does. The KJV's 'or to thy faithfulness round about thee?' mistakes the sentence for another question; it is a statement.

philological_notes.note: A rare adjective, 'mighty, strong', found only here; related to chason, 'strong' (Amos 2:9).
'Around you', in the sense of a surrounding retinue. God's faithfulness is pictured as his guard.

verses.translation_literal: You are ruling over the swelling of the sea; when its waves lift, you, you calm them.
verses.translation_dramatic: You rule the swelling sea. When its waves heave up, it is you, you alone, who bring them down to stillness.
verses.directors_commentary: To an ancient audience the sea is not scenery but chaos: the Canaanite myths make Yam, Sea, a rival god whom the storm-god must defeat for kingship. Here the psalm says that YHWH needs no battle; he rules the swell, and the waves only rise so that he may quiet them. 'Ge'ut' is the 'swelling' of pride, the same word as 'majesty' or 'arrogance', so the sea is personified as proud. The KJV 'raging' is an interpretation; the Hebrew says 'pride/swelling'. The pronoun 'you' is stressed twice, 'you... you', as a contrast with every other power, that is the polemic against the sea-gods. 'Teshabbechem' (you calm them) is a rare verb of soothing, used again in Psalm 65:8 for stilling the roar of the seas, as Rashi cites. Radak and Meiri tie it to the Red Sea.

philological_notes.note: 'Swelling, pride, majesty'. The sea is credited with pride, so that the verse makes YHWH its ruler.
Piel of a root meaning 'to still, calm', not the more common 'to praise'. Compare 'who calms the roar of the seas' (Ps 65:8).

verses.translation_literal: You, you crushed Rahab like the slain; with the arm of your strength you scattered your enemies.
verses.translation_dramatic: You crushed Rahab, and she lay like a corpse. With the arm of your strength you scattered your enemies.
verses.directors_commentary: Now the sea-battle is named. Rahab is the sea monster of Israel's poetry, the chaos-dragon defeated at creation (Job 9:13; 26:12; Isa 51:9). Treat 'Rahab' as a name the audience knows and fears. The KJV leaves 'Rahab' unexplained, and then adds 'in pieces', which is not in the Hebrew: the verb 'dakka' is simply 'to crush'. The simile 'like the slain' (kechalal) means a corpse, someone struck down and lying. The strongest note is the hand: 'the arm of your strength' is a royal image of the king's power in war. Later tradition (Rashi, Radak, the Targum) reads Rahab as Egypt and Pharaoh, so that the verse becomes the Exodus, but the poem's imagery is older: the defeat of chaos before the founding of the world, a kinship with the Near Eastern combat myth, with Israel's God doing alone what Baal and Marduk do with help.

philological_notes.note: The mythic sea monster of chaos; a poetic name for Egypt in Isaiah 30:7. The root means 'to be arrogant, bluster', so the name carries pride as well.
'You crushed', written with aleph where the pattern of the verb ending in he would expect yod; the commentators note the irregular spelling.

verses.translation_literal: To you, heaven; also to you, earth; the world and its fullness, you, you founded them.
verses.translation_dramatic: The heavens are yours, and the earth is yours as well. The world, and everything that fills it: you laid its foundations, you.
verses.directors_commentary: The long hymn reaches its summit with a deed of title: ownership by creation. Say it slowly, as a man reads the boundaries of an estate. The heavens, the earth, the 'tevel' (the inhabited, fertile world) and 'its fullness' (all that fills it) belong to the one who 'founded' them, the same architectural language as the 'building' of verses 3 and 5. The KJV's 'as for the world and the fulness thereof' adds a phrase of its own, softening an emphatic shout into a lecture. In the ancient Near East a god's temple was the sign of his ownership, and here the whole cosmos is that house. The stress on 'you' (atah) at the end is the same as in the previous two verses: three times in a row, 'you'. The psalm has built an argument: the God who is owner and founder of everything has also bound himself to David, and that is why what follows, in verse 39 on, will be so shocking.

philological_notes.note: 'The inhabited, fertile world', as distinct from 'eretz', the earth as a whole.
'You founded them', the verb of laying a foundation, which belongs to the same field of building images as 'yibaneh' (v. 3) and 'uvaniti' (v. 5).

verses.translation_literal: [The] north and [the] south, you, you created them; Tabor and Hermon, at your name they shout for joy.
verses.translation_dramatic: North and south, the whole stretch of the map: you made them, you, and no one else. And look where the land rises. Tabor in the west, Hermon in the far north, two great shoulders of stone, and they cry out for joy the moment your name is spoken.
verses.directors_commentary:
The poet walks the compass: north and south frame the world, and two mountains stand as its witnesses. Tabor rises like a dome over the Jezreel plain; Hermon, snow-capped even in summer, is the highest summit anyone in Israel could see. Both were holy heights to neighbouring peoples, and Hermon and the northern mountain Zaphon belonged to the storm-god Baal in Canaanite myth. The verse takes that geography back: these peaks did not belong to a rival, they were created, and they sing for YHWH.

Two things the KJV smooths. First, 'created' is bara, the verb kept for God's creating, and the pronoun 'you' comes first: 'you, you created them', a flat denial that any other power did. Second, yamin is 'south' only because the speaker faces east and the right hand points south; the same word returns in the next verse as 'right hand'. KJV also turns the present 'they shout for joy' into a future, 'shall rejoice', and softens ranan, a ringing cry, into quiet rejoicing.

philological_notes.note: 'Right hand', and so 'south' for one who faces the sunrise; the same word names the right hand in v14, and the echo ties the geography of creation to the arm of the Creator.
A ringing, shouted cry of joy, here said of mountains. The imperfect is habitual, not a future promise: whenever the name is invoked, they cry out.

verses.translation_literal: To you [belongs] an arm with might; your hand is strong, your right hand is high.
verses.translation_dramatic: The strength is yours. An arm, and in it a warrior's might. Your hand is strong; your right hand is raised, high above everything that stands below it.
verses.directors_commentary:
In the ancient Near East a king's power was pictured as his arm and hand, and a raised right hand was the gesture of victory and oath. Here the poet lets the mountains fall silent and sets the body of God in front of us: arm, hand, right hand, three stages of one gesture, drawn back, closed, lifted.

The KJV's 'a mighty arm' turns a phrase into an adjective. The Hebrew says 'to you an arm with might': the arm comes accompanied by might, and the sentence opens on 'to you', a claim of ownership, as v19 does. The verb 'is high' is the root rum, which will return in vv17, 18 and 20 for the lifting of the people and of David. What is true of God's right hand is promised to those who stand under it.

philological_notes.note: 'It is lifted high'. The root recurs in vv17, 18 and 20; the height of God's hand is what raises his people and his chosen king.

verses.translation_literal: Righteousness and justice [are the] foundation of your throne; covenant loyalty and faithfulness come to meet your face.
verses.translation_dramatic: But the throne does not rest on force. Under it, righteousness and justice, laid like stone. And before it, walking ahead to meet your face, loyalty and truth.
verses.directors_commentary:
A throne in the ancient world was a seat of judgment as much as of rule: the king sat to hear cases, and a dynasty claimed to rest on justice. The verse sets the throne on a base, makhon, a fixed, prepared place, and sends two servants running in front of it, as heralds go ahead of a king.

The KJV 'habitation' mistranslates makhon, which is a foundation, a settled site (the same root, kun, returns in v22 when God's hand 'will be established' with David). 'Mercy' for chesed loses its force: it is covenant loyalty, the kept promise, which is the theme of the whole psalm; 'truth' for emet is faithfulness, reliability. 'Go before thy face' is also tame: yekaddemu is 'come to meet', 'confront', so these are not a retinue walking behind but forces that arrive first to receive the King.

philological_notes.note: A fixed base or prepared place, not a 'habitation'. Same root as tikkon in v22: the throne and the king's helping hand are both 'established'.
Covenant loyalty and faithfulness, the pair that carries the psalm from v2 onward. Here they are personified as attendants who arrive before the throne.

verses.translation_literal: How blessed [is] the people knowing the shout of joy; YHWH, in the light of your face they walk.
verses.translation_dramatic: Happy the people who know the shout, who have heard the horn go up and known what it means. LORD, they walk in the light of your face.
verses.directors_commentary:
Teruah is the sound of Israel's assembly: the blast of the ram's horn at festival and in battle, the roar that greets a king. The same word is used of Balaam's report that 'the shout of a king is among them'. To 'know' it is not to understand a term but to have been in the crowd when it went up. KJV's 'the joyful sound' empties it into a pleasant noise; it is a loud, communal acclamation of the divine king, and carries a note of war.

The second half is a procession, not a metaphor for cheerfulness. 'The light of your face' is the radiance of a king who looks on his subjects with favour, and 'they walk' is a habitual, continuing action (the verb ends in an extra -n, a form that lends the walking a habitual, steady tone, which KJV flattens to 'shall walk'). Rashi hears the horn of the New Year; Radak and Meiri the battle shout of a people whose king marches with them.

philological_notes.note: A shout or blast: festival acclamation, horn blast and war cry at once. It is the cry for the king in Numbers 23:21, which Radak and Meiri cite here.
'The light of your face': a king's favour as radiance on those who stand before him. Ibn Ezra compares the poet's phrase to 'by his light I walk through darkness'.

verses.translation_literal: In your name they exult all the day, and in your righteousness they are lifted up.
verses.translation_dramatic: All day long they exult in your name. And in your righteousness they are lifted up, raised from the dust to stand upright.
verses.directors_commentary:
'All the day' is not a figure of speech for 'often'. A day in the ancient world ran from sunrise to sunset, and this people's rejoicing keeps pace with it. The Hebrew gives the verb of rejoicing, gil, which is a spinning, leaping joy, and no object other than the Name: to speak YHWH's name is to celebrate.

Two small repairs to the KJV. 'Shall rejoice' and 'shall be exalted' are futures; the Hebrew is a present, habitual: this is what the people do. And 'exalted' is the same verb, rum, that opened the thread in v14 for God's right hand: the height of the hand becomes the height of the people. Notice the wordplay with righteousness, tzedaqah: the people are raised not by their own right standing but by God's.

philological_notes.note: 'They are lifted up', the passive-sense counterpart of God's raised right hand in v14; the root runs through vv14, 17, 18 and 20.

verses.translation_literal: For [the] splendor of their strength [are] you, and in your favor our horn is lifted up.
verses.translation_dramatic: For you are the glory of their strength. Whatever they have, you are its brightness. And when you are pleased with us, our horn goes up.
verses.directors_commentary:
The horn is the picture of a bull or ram lifting its head: strength, status, and in a royal psalm the dynasty itself (Meiri reads it as the monarchy). To say 'our horn is lifted up' is to say that the king holds his head high among rivals; to say it 'in your favour' is to say he does not hold it up himself.

The verse swings from 'their' to 'our' and the KJV rightly keeps both, but its 'the glory of their strength' hides a nuance: tiferet is a beauty worn like a crown, the ornament of strength, and Ibn Ezra's point is that they do not boast in their own might but in yours. Ratzon, 'favour', is the king's pleased willingness, the opposite of the stern face that gives no audience. There is also a spelling question in the last verb: the written text has 'you lift up our horn' and the reading has 'our horn is lifted up'; both put the action in God's hands.

philological_notes.note: 'Our horn': the horn of an ox or ram as the emblem of strength and rank. The plural suffix 'our' with a singular verb is explained by Radak and Meiri as 'each of our horns', that is, each king of Israel.
Splendor or glory, the adornment of strength. Ibn Ezra: they take pride not in their own strength but in God's.

verses.translation_literal: For to YHWH [belongs] our shield, and to the Holy One of Israel our king.
verses.translation_dramatic: Our shield belongs to the LORD. Our king belongs to the Holy One of Israel. We hold nothing of our own.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse is a pair of ownership claims, each opened by the little word 'to': our shield is YHWH's; our king is the Holy One of Israel's. The KJV 'the Lord is our defence' turns the possessive into an equation and loses the point: the king is not merely under protection, he is the property of God. In the ancient Near East the king was commonly called a shield of his people, and the poet answers with a claim of the highest kind: whatever shield or king Israel has, he is God's.

'Defence' is also soft for magen, the actual shield, a hard leather-and-bronze barrier in front of the body. 'The Holy One of Israel' is a title chiefly from Isaiah: God set apart, the very opposite of the cult-pillars and king-statues of Israel's neighbours. Ibn Ezra and Radak identify the king here as David and his line; Malbim sets the shield against the miracles worked through the royal house.

philological_notes.note: A shield, not 'defence'. It was the standard image for protection, and in some poetry a title for a ruler who shields the people.
The lamed of possession is repeated: the shield 'belongs to' YHWH, the king 'belongs to' the Holy One. KJV and BBE render only the second half as a plain possessive and the first as an equation.

verses.translation_literal: Then you spoke in a vision to your faithful ones, and you said: I have set help upon a warrior; I have raised up a chosen one from [the] people.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then you spoke, in a vision, to those who were faithful to you. You said: I have set help upon a warrior. I have lifted up one chosen out of the people.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm turns from praise to promise: now God is quoted, in the first person, and what follows (vv20 to 38) recalls the covenant with David. 'Then' points back to the day of the choosing. The commentators disagree on who 'your faithful ones' were: Rashi names Nathan and Gad; Radak and Metzudat David say Samuel; Meiri also thinks of Jacob's blessing of Judah. What is clear is the form: a prophetic vision, not a private thought.

The KJV 'thy holy one', singular, has changed the plural chasidim, 'your faithful ones', the people who keep covenant loyalty (chesed) with God. 'Laid help upon' is exact: God places help like a load on a shoulder. 'One that is mighty' is gibbor, a warrior, not an abstract 'mighty man'. The last clause has an upward motion: 'I raised up', again the root rum of v14 and v17. The 'chosen one' (bachur) is also the word for a young man of fighting age, and it sets one against the whole people: the choice is made 'from the people', not by them.

philological_notes.note: 'To your faithful ones', plural, from chasid, the person who answers chesed with chesed. KJV 'thy holy one' flattens this to one prophet.
'I have set help', 'I have laid help'. Malbim reads the verb as setting something in proportion to what is fitting to it.
A chosen, picked man; also the word for a young man. Ibn Ezra takes it as 'chosen' (like nivchar), or as one who is so in his kingship.

verses.translation_literal: I have found David, my servant; with the oil of my holiness I have anointed him.
verses.translation_dramatic: I have found David. My servant. I have poured over him the oil of my holiness, and marked him as mine.
verses.directors_commentary:
'I have found' is the language of a search: God has looked over the field and discovered the man, as one finds a lost sheep or a treasure. David is introduced not as 'king' but as 'my servant', ebed, the title of a vassal who answers to a great king; that is the status in which the covenant is made.

The oil is the anointing oil of the sanctuary, prepared with fixed spices and kept for the sacred (it is called 'holy anointing oil' in the law). The KJV's 'holy oil' is right in sense but loses the structure: the Hebrew says 'oil of my holiness', the oil that belongs to God and is set apart by him; anointing with it is a transfer of ownership. In the surrounding world a king was installed by being seated on a throne or crowned; Israel's king is marked with oil, a priestly rite, and the Hebrew word 'messiah' simply means 'anointed one'.

philological_notes.note: 'Oil of my holiness': the sanctuary's anointing oil, which belongs to God. Radak identifies it with the oil called the oil of holy anointing.
'I have found': Ibn Ezra and Radak read this as 'none like him was found in his generation'; Metzudat David reads it as the finding of David among Jesse's sons.

verses.translation_literal: With whom my hand will be steadfast; also my arm will strengthen him.
verses.translation_dramatic: My hand will stand firm beside him. My arm, too, will make him strong.
verses.directors_commentary:
The hand and arm of v14 reappear, now turned toward one man. 'My hand' stands next to David as a companion, and 'my arm' is the strength behind it. The two parts are not a repetition: the hand does the work and the arm, the upper limb, is the force that moves it.

The verb tikkon is the root kun, 'to be firm, fixed', the same root as the 'foundation' (makhon) of the throne in v15: God's hand and God's throne are both made firm, so David's kingship rests on both. The KJV's 'with whom my hand shall be established' is correct but heavy, and it translates a plain preposition ('with him', 'beside him') as though it were an abstract relation. Radak and Metzudat David take 'my hand will be steadfast with him' as: it will stand ready to help him.

philological_notes.note: 'It will be firm, established'; the root of makhon in v15. The throne's base and the helping hand are one idea.
'It will strengthen him', 'make him bold'; the piel is intensive. Metzudat David: so that he overcomes his enemies further.

verses.translation_literal: [An] enemy will not exact [from] him, and a son of injustice will not afflict him.
verses.translation_dramatic: No enemy will press him for what he owes. No son of injustice will bend him down.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is a hard verse, and the first verb carries the difficulty. Yashi can come from a root that means 'to deceive' (BBE: 'the deceit of those who are against him'), or from nasha, 'to lend on credit, to exact a debt' (Exodus 22:24, the word for the creditor, nosheh). Rashi, Radak, Metzudat David and Metzudat Zion all take the second sense, and so do KJV and ASV: no enemy will treat the king as a debtor to be squeezed for tribute. Meiri keeps both. That reading fits the world: an ancient king's rivals extracted tribute, and a vassal could be bled by a creditor-nation.

The second half is clearer. 'Son of injustice' is a Hebrew idiom for a man defined by wrongdoing, as 'son of worth' is a man of worth; the KJV 'son of wickedness' keeps it. 'Afflict' (anah) is oppression and humbling. The rhythm is a pair of negatives, one for the enemy outside who demands, one for the bully who crushes. The promise echoes a very similar word in the Nathan oracle (2 Samuel 7:10), where 'sons of wickedness' are said not to afflict Israel any more.

philological_notes.note: Either 'he will exact as a creditor' (nasha, as in Rashi's citation of Exodus 22:24) or 'he will deceive' (nasha II). I take the first. Ibn Ezra reports both.
'Son of injustice': a person marked by wrongdoing. Meiri understands it as the other nations.

verses.translation_literal: And I will crush his opponents from before him, and those who hate him I will strike down.
verses.translation_dramatic: And I will break his adversaries before his eyes. Those who hate him, I will strike them down.
verses.directors_commentary:
The promise turns from defence to attack, and God speaks in the first person: 'I will crush', 'I will strike down'. 'From before him' means in his presence: the king is to see it done, a standard picture of victory in a royal ideology where the king's enemies fall in front of his throne.

The verbs are strong. Katat is to pound, to beat small, what is done to grain in a mortar and to idols that are smashed; the KJV 'beat down' is milder. Nagaf is a blow that fells, the verb used of a plague or of Israel's defeat in battle, and Metzudat Zion ties it to the noun for plague; the KJV's 'plague them' is correct in sense but archaic, and it hides that this is a blow, not a disease. Malbim reads the second half as being struck with a plague that makes the haters shunned. The pairing of 'opponents' (tzarim, those who press in) and 'haters' (misanim) names enemies by what they do and what they feel.

philological_notes.note: 'To crush, to pound small'; Metzudat Zion: crushing and breaking.
'I will strike down'; the verb belongs with the noun for plague (negef). Metzudat Zion links it to magefah.

verses.translation_literal: And my faithfulness and my covenant loyalty [are] with him, and in my name his horn will be lifted high.
verses.translation_dramatic: My faithfulness walks beside him, and my loyal love will not leave his side. Where my name is spoken over him, his horn rises high.
verses.directors_commentary:
God is still speaking, and the voice must stay steady and warm: this is the Lord recalling the oath he made to David, and the two great covenant words, emunah and chesed, arrive together as a pair, 'faithfulness' and 'covenant loyalty', with the same pairing that frames the whole psalm. The KJV's 'mercy' for chesed is too soft; the word names the loyalty owed inside a bond, not pity for the weak.

The 'horn' is a bull's or ram's horn, the ancient picture of strength and victory. To 'lift' it is to give a man standing, and 'in my name' says that this standing is borrowed from God, not won by the king's own arm. Say it as a promise of backing, not a boast.

philological_notes.note: 'His horn': an animal's horn as the emblem of strength, dignity and victory; its being raised (תרום) means that the king prevails and is honoured. The same image appears in Ps 89:18.

A fixed pair of covenant words, 'my reliability' and 'my covenant loyalty'. Malbim divides them into what God does for the king's deeds and what he does from free choice; this is his scheme, not a lexical sense.

verses.translation_literal: And I will set on the sea his hand, and on the rivers his right [hand].
verses.translation_dramatic: I will lay his hand upon the sea, and his right hand upon the rivers. Let the waters that terrify others learn his grip.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the verse where the king's reach becomes cosmic. 'Sea' (yam) and 'rivers' (neharot) are not only geography: in Canaanite myth Yam and Nahar are the same chaos-god, whom Baal defeats, and the psalm has already said that the Lord rules the raging sea (v. 10). To put David's hand on them is to hand him a share of that victory. Do not play it as a simple map of trade routes, though Radak reads it so, citing Hiram of Tyre's gifts by sea and Aramean tributes from across the river.

The KJV's 'in the sea' and 'in the rivers' make the hand sound as if it were dipped or lost in water; the Hebrew preposition is 'on', a hand laid upon something to rule it. The 'right hand' is the hand of power, and the pairing of hand and right hand is a parallelism, not two body parts.

philological_notes.note: 'On the sea': also the name of the sea-god Yam in Ugaritic myth; with 'rivers' it recalls the defeated chaos waters, so the verse is more than a statement about geography.
'I will set' (perfect with waw-consecutive, a future promise); the same verb recurs in v. 30, 'I will establish'.

verses.translation_literal: He, he will call out to me: My father [are] you, my God and rock of my salvation.
verses.translation_dramatic: He will cry out to me, and this is what he will say: You are my father. My God, and the rock where I am saved.
verses.directors_commentary:
The king's own words are quoted inside God's speech, and this is the emotional centre of the passage: not a throne-room formula but a son's cry. The line is nearly a liturgy, three titles in one breath: father, God, rock of salvation. The KJV's 'He shall cry unto me' is fine, but 'cry' hides that the verb is simply 'call', and the Hebrew puts the pronoun first ('he, he will call'), stressing that it is this man, and no other, who will call.

In the ancient Near East a king was often called the 'son' of his god; here it is a covenant relation of obedience and care, as Meiri and Metzudat David read it, a child's trust in his father. 'Rock' (tsur) pictures a cliff to flee to in war and storm, and it is also a divine title elsewhere in Israel's poetry.

philological_notes.note: 'My father [are] you': the adoption formula of the Davidic covenant (2 Sam 7:14 'I will be his father'); here it is returned by the king as a confession.
'Rock': a crag or cliff, a place of safety and a divine title; Metzudat Zion glosses it as 'firmness'.

token_glosses.gloss: he will call out to me

verses.translation_literal: Also I, firstborn I will make him, most high to the kings of [the] earth.
verses.translation_dramatic: And I, for my part, will make him my firstborn, the highest of all the kings of the earth.
verses.directors_commentary:
The 'also I' answers the king's cry in the verse before: he calls God 'father', and God replies by naming him 'firstborn'. Give the 'I' its weight. In the ancient world the firstborn held the double portion and the right of rule, so this is a legal title as much as a tender one. David, in fact, was the youngest of Jesse's sons; the title is given, not inherited.

The KJV's 'higher than the kings of the earth' reads 'most high' (elyon) as a comparison; the Hebrew has the very word that is the title of God himself, 'Most High', so the king is made the highest among the human kings, under God. The KJV's 'also I will make him my firstborn' is correct but flattens the sound: 'ani' with its long vowel here, as Radak and Meiri note, is a stressed pause form.

philological_notes.note: 'Firstborn': the son with the right of rule and the larger inheritance; here a title of rank given by adoption, since David was not the firstborn of his own family.
'Most high': also a standard title of God (Ps 7:18; 47:3); said of the king, it marks him as the first among earthly rulers.

verses.translation_literal: For ever I will keep for him my covenant loyalty, and my covenant [will be] reliable to him.
verses.translation_dramatic: Forever I will keep my loving loyalty for him, and my covenant with him will stand firm.
verses.directors_commentary:
'Forever' opens the line, and the actor should let it hang before the rest. This is the first of a run of verses where the promise is stated in its strongest form: God will 'keep' (shamar), as one guards a treasure, his chesed for David. The KJV's 'mercy' again loses the covenant sense; chesed is what a partner owes in a bond.

The word 'covenant' (berit) in the ancient Near East is a treaty, usually between a great king and his vassal, sealed with an oath. Here the great king binds himself. 'Reliable' (ne'emenet) is the passive of the verb from which 'amen' comes: something on which one can lean and not fall.

philological_notes.note: 'Reliable, trustworthy': a niphal participle of the root of 'amen' and 'faithfulness'; the covenant is something one can lean on.

verses.translation_literal: And I will set for ever his seed, and his throne like the days of [the] heavens.
verses.translation_dramatic: I will set his offspring in place for ever, and his throne will last as long as the days of the heavens.
verses.directors_commentary:
The promise now passes from the king to his line. 'Seed' (zera) is a collective: all the descendants, not one son. The throne is compared to 'the days of the heavens': as long as the sky stays over the earth. The KJV's 'his seed also will I make to endure' adds an 'endure' that is not in the Hebrew; the verb is the same 'set' (sim) as in verse 26, and the line says only that God will place them 'for ever'.

Play the image as something an ancient listener could look at: the unchanging sky over the hills was the standing picture of permanence. Meiri ties the verse to Nathan's oracle in 1 Chronicles 17 ('I will establish his throne for ever'), and the psalm is, throughout, an argument with that promise.

philological_notes.note: 'Like the days of the heavens': a standard phrase for what lasts as long as the sky (Deut 11:21); the throne is given the heavens' own age.

verses.translation_literal: If his sons forsake my torah, and in my judgments they do not walk,
verses.translation_dramatic: But if his sons turn away from my law, if they will not walk in my judgments,
verses.directors_commentary:
Here the voice must change. After the long swell of 'for ever', the line begins with 'if', and the actor should drop, almost to a lowered voice: this is the condition, the shadow inside the promise. The speech does not say that the king's house will be perfect; it says what God will do when it is not.

The KJV's 'children' for 'sons' is a small softening; the Hebrew is the plain 'his sons', the heirs to the throne. 'Torah' means instruction, not a code alone, and 'walk' is the Hebrew picture of a whole way of life. 'Judgments' (mishpatim) are the rulings of the king-as-judge, which is why Ibn Ezra notes that the verse names them: the king is the nation's chief judge. The Davidic promise is conditional on conduct in the line of Psalm 132:12, but unconditional in what it finally keeps, as the next verses will show.

philological_notes.note: 'My instruction': the noun comes from the verb 'to throw, direct, teach'; it is wider than 'law' alone.
'They will walk': the form carries a paragogic nun, a poetic ending; 'to walk' is the Bible's regular metaphor for conduct.

verses.translation_literal: If my statutes they profane, and my commandments they do not keep,
verses.translation_dramatic: If they profane my statutes, if my commandments go unkept,
verses.directors_commentary:
The second half of the condition, in the same cadence: two lines, two kinds of failure. The KJV's 'break' for chalal misses the Hebrew. The verb means to 'profane' or 'pollute', to make a holy thing common, and it is the word used of defiling the sanctuary; it will return in verse 35 with God as its subject, 'I will not profane my covenant'. The pair is deliberate: God will not do what the sons do.

The statutes (chuqqim) are the fixed ordinances, the commandments (mitzvot) the particular orders. Ibn Ezra takes the first as the prohibitions and the second as the positive commands. The 'keep' (shamar) in the last line is the same verb as in verse 29: God 'keeps' his loyalty, the sons do not 'keep' his commandments, and the contrast is the point.

philological_notes.note: 'They profane': piel of חלל, to make common or defile; the KJV's 'break' loses the sacral sense. God uses the same verb of himself, negated, in v. 35.

verses.translation_literal: Then I will visit with a rod their transgression, and with plagues their iniquity.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then I will call their rebellion to account, and the rod will fall; their guilt I will answer with blows.
verses.directors_commentary:
The answer comes, and it is harsh: the rod and the plague. Do not soften it. The Hebrew 'paqad' is the verb of an official who inspects and counts; to 'visit' something upon someone is to call it to account, which is why the KJV's 'visit' is accurate, though it sounds today like a social call. The 'rod' (shevet) is both a father's stick of discipline and a king's sceptre, which is the point here: a father disciplines the son he has not disowned. This is the theology of Nathan's oracle in 2 Samuel 7:14, 'with the rod of men and with the blows of the sons of Adam'.

The KJV's 'stripes' for nega'im is old and vague; the Hebrew word is 'plagues' or 'strokes', the term used for blows and for the afflictions of the body, including skin disease. Rashi reads the rod as Rezon and the plagues as the demon Ashmedai, an old midrash, and Radak and Metzudat David read them as defeat by enemies and loss of kingship; the verse itself names only rod and plague.

philological_notes.note: 'I will visit, call to account': the verb of inspection and reckoning; Metzudat Zion takes a sense of 'lack', which is not the sense followed here.
'With a rod': both a father's disciplinary stick and a ruler's sceptre; it echoes Prov 23:13-14.
'Their transgression': rebellion against an authority, a breach of the covenant; paired with 'iniquity' (avon).

verses.translation_literal: But my covenant loyalty I will not break off from with him, and I will not deal falsely with my faithfulness.
verses.translation_dramatic: But my loyal love I will never tear away from him, and I will not betray my faithfulness.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the turn, the great 'but'. The voice that has just promised the rod now rises again, and the verse repeats the first two words of the speech, chesed and emunah, to close the circle with verse 25. The KJV's 'nevertheless' supplies the contrast the Hebrew leaves to the listener: the line starts only with 'and', and the contrast is carried by the sense.

The verb 'afir' is rare, from a root meaning 'to break, annul', and the KJV's 'utterly take from him' imports 'utterly'; it is a hiphil, 'I will break off', and the phrase 'from with him' means to cut loose an attachment. 'Deal falsely' (shaqer) is the vocabulary of treaty-breaking: a vassal or a king who lies in his word. Radak reads chesed here as the kingship itself.

philological_notes.note: 'I will break off, annul': hiphil of פור; the KJV's 'utterly take' is an interpretation, and Metzudat Zion links it to breaking and cancelling a covenant.
'I will deal falsely': piel of שקר, to act as a liar; the opposite of emunah, so the verse ends on the word it began the speech with.

verses.translation_literal: I will not profane my covenant, and the utterance of my lips I will not change.
verses.translation_dramatic: I will not profane my covenant. What has left my lips I will not change.
verses.directors_commentary:
Now the speech reaches its hardest edge: the word given cannot be taken back. 'Profane' (chalel) is the same verb used in verse 32 of the sons' crime; God says he will not do to the covenant what they do to the statutes. The KJV's 'break' hides this answer between the two verses. The actor can say the verb the same way twice.

An ancient word was believed to be a thing with its own power: once spoken, especially in an oath, it could not be recalled. 'The utterance of my lips' (motsa sefatai) is the thing that has gone out from the lips, as the KJV rightly has. The verb 'change' (shanah) is the same as for altering a decree, so it is a legal term as well. Malbim sees the line as answering the 'I have sworn to David my servant' of verse 4.

philological_notes.note: 'What goes out of my lips': a spoken word treated as an object that has left the speaker and cannot be recalled; compare Num 30:3 and Deut 23:24.

verses.translation_literal: One [thing] I have sworn by my holiness: if to David I lie [may I be cursed].
verses.translation_dramatic: Once, and once for all, I have sworn by my own holiness: if I lie to David, let it be on me.
verses.directors_commentary:
The climax of the divine speech is an oath, and the actor must hear its grammar. 'If to David I lie' is the old oath formula in which the curse is left unspoken: 'if I do this, [may something terrible happen to me]'. The KJV, ASV and Webster turn it into a plain 'I will not lie', which is the sense but loses the force; the Hebrew has God place himself under the curse. Metzudat David notes that the Bible commonly leaves such curses unsaid, as in Psalm 95:11, 'if they enter my rest'.

'By my holiness': God has no greater power to swear by, so he swears by his own holy nature (as in Amos 4:2). 'Once' (achat) can mean 'once for all' or 'one thing alone'; Malbim reads it as 'a single oath without conditions', and Radak as 'one oath, which I will not change'. The name David is spoken last in the verse, and the line should fall on it.

philological_notes.note: An oath formula with the curse suppressed: 'if I lie to David [then may I…]'; it asserts the opposite, 'I will certainly not lie'.
'Once, one [thing]': either 'once for all' or 'one single oath'; the commentators differ, and both senses fit.
'By my holiness': God swears by his own nature, having nothing greater; compare Amos 4:2 and Heb 6:13 for the idea.

verses.translation_literal: His seed — to forever he will be; and his throne [is] like the sun before me.
verses.translation_dramatic: His line will go on for ever. And his throne? A sun that never leaves my sight.
verses.directors_commentary:
God is speaking, quoting the covenant oath of the first half of the psalm. The verse is a promise of permanence, and its images are chosen with care. The sun is the most reliable thing in the ancient sky, and in Egypt and Mesopotamia it was also the god of justice and the emblem of kingship; to say the king's throne is 'like the sun' is to give royal ideology to the house of David, with YHWH, not Shamash or Re, as the guarantor. Say the line steadily, as a man reading a will.

The KJV 'his seed shall endure for ever' supplies a verb; the Hebrew has the plain 'will be' (yihyeh), and the KJV's 'his throne as the sun' drops the verb altogether, as the Hebrew does. 'Seed' (zera') means descendants as a line, which matters in a dynasty. The last word, 'before me' (negdi), puts the throne under God's eye: Radak takes it as 'as long as the sun lasts', Metzudat David as 'God watching over it'. Both are in the word.

philological_notes.note: 'His seed': the royal line, not only one son. The promise is to the dynasty, which is why the fall of the monarchy, described in the next verses, tests the psalm.
'Before me', 'in front of me': under God's gaze. Metzudat David reads it as God watching over the throne.

verses.translation_literal: Like the moon it will be established for ever; and a witness in the sky [is] faithful. Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: Like the moon, fixed for all time — and up there in the sky a witness who does not lie. Selah.
verses.directors_commentary:
The sun gave way to the moon, and the second image is gentler: the moon waxes, wanes and vanishes, yet always returns. Radak hears exactly that: the line may shine or go dark, but it does not end. Do not hurry; the speaker is pointing upward.

The KJV 'as a faithful witness in heaven' makes the witness an extra comparison. In the Hebrew there is no 'as' before 'witness' and no verb: 'a witness in the sky [is] faithful'. Who is the witness? Rashi and Radak say the moon (and sun, with Jer 33:20-21 in mind); others take the sky itself, or God, as the witness. Keep the ambiguity and let the sky carry the oath, because in the ancient Near East treaties were sworn before the heavenly bodies. 'Sky' (shachak) is literally the thin, dust-like fine expanse, and 'heaven' for it is the KJV's habit. Selah marks a pause, probably for an instrumental passage or a lifting of the voice.

philological_notes.note: 'Will be established', a niphal: set firmly in place. Ibn Ezra says the subject returns to 'his seed' or the throne, and 'for ever' (olam) is adverbial.
'A witness in the sky is faithful': a verbless clause with no 'as'. Rashi reads the moon and sun as witnesses of the covenant, citing Jeremiah 33:20-21; Radak reads the moon alone.
A musical or liturgical marker of uncertain meaning, probably a pause or interlude; left untranslated.

verses.translation_literal: But you — you have spurned, and you have rejected; you have been furious with your anointed.
verses.translation_dramatic: But you. You! You have thrown him aside. You have turned from him in disgust. Your fury has fallen on the one you anointed.
verses.directors_commentary:
The whole psalm turns here on two words, 'But you' (ve'attah). Until now the singer has recited what God swore; now he accuses God to his face. The pivot should land like a slammed door: after thirty-six verses of praise, the actors drop the music. Radak insists the poet is not charging God with breaking the oath but protesting, in astonishment, at how long it has lasted.

The KJV 'cast off and abhorred' and 'wroth' are fair, but 'abhorred' is stronger than the verb ma'as, 'to reject, refuse as worthless', which is what one does with a spoiled offering. The third verb, hit'abbarta, from 'ebrah (overflow, rage), means that fury has spilled over: it is a rage that crosses a border. 'Anointed' (mashiach) is the king himself, consecrated with oil, and in this context the ruler on David's throne, for whom Rashi names Zedekiah and Metzudat David the same king; the psalm does not name him. The pronoun 'you' is stressed in Hebrew, which does not need it.

philological_notes.note: 'You have spurned': to cast off, treat as a thing thrown away. The same verb appears in laments for Israel as a whole (Psalm 44:10, 60:3).
'You have been furious': a hitpael of the root for 'cross over, overflow', hence 'to boil over with 'ebrah (wrath)'. Metzudat Zion glosses it as anger and rage.
'Your anointed': the king consecrated by oil. Rashi and Metzudat David identify him with Zedekiah, the last king of Judah; Radak with David himself.

verses.translation_literal: You have repudiated the covenant of your servant; you have profaned his consecrated crown to the ground.
verses.translation_dramatic: The covenant you swore to your servant — you have torn it up. His crown, set apart for you, lies defiled in the dust.
verses.directors_commentary:
The accusation is now specific, and legal: a covenant (berit) is a sworn bond, and to 'repudiate' it is to treat the oath as nothing. The speaker uses the very word 'servant' ('avdekha) that God used of David earlier in the psalm, so God is being held to his own language. The singer is not insulting; he is citing.

The KJV 'made void' for ne'artah is a guess at a very rare verb, found only here and in Lamentations 2:7, where the Lord 'has disowned his sanctuary'. Ibn Ezra, Radak and Meiri link the two places, and a link with ruin or disowning is the safest ground. The KJV 'by casting it to the ground' adds a method; the Hebrew simply sets 'profaned' and 'to the ground' side by side. 'Crown' translates nezer, the consecrated diadem, from a root meaning 'set apart': the high priest's headband is also called a nezer. So profaning it is a sacrilege, not only a loss. The crown goes to the dust, the throne of verse 37 to the ground in verse 45.

philological_notes.note: A rare verb, found elsewhere only in Lamentations 2:7 ('he has disowned his sanctuary'). Ibn Ezra and Meiri connect the two and take it as 'destroy, spoil'; Metzudat Zion as 'cast far away'; Rashi 'you annulled'. 'Repudiated' keeps the sense of disowning.
'His consecrated crown': nezer, a diadem of dedication, from the root 'to set apart'. Metzudat Zion and Meiri simply gloss it 'his crown'. The STEPBible lemma (נָסָה) is an error.

verses.translation_literal: You have breached all his walls; you have made his strongholds a ruin.
verses.translation_dramatic: Every wall he built, you have broken through. His fortresses are rubble and dust.
verses.directors_commentary:
The poem now moves from the crown to the country. A king's security was measured in walls and strongholds, built at great expense and by forced labour; to have them 'breached' is to have the kingdom opened like a ripped sack. Let the voice drop to a flat, exhausted list.

The KJV 'hedges' for gederot is archaic and wrong for the scene: a gederah is a stone wall or enclosure (Metzudat Zion: a wall, a partition), the dry-stone barrier of sheepfolds and vineyards as well as of towns. 'Hedges' makes the king a gardener. The verb parats, 'breach, burst through', is the verb for a flood or a siege breaking a wall, and God is the grammatical subject: it is God who breaks, not the invader. Malbim and Meiri make the enemies an agent; the Hebrew does not mention them. Mechittah, 'ruin' or 'terror', is cousin to the word for being shattered or panicked, so the fortresses are not simply lost but frightened to pieces. The KJV 'brought to ruin' is adequate.

philological_notes.note: 'His walls': a gederah is a built enclosure of stone, a wall or partition (Metzudat Zion), not a living hedge.
'Ruin, shattering': from the root for being broken or dismayed. Metzudat Zion compares Jeremiah 51:56 ('their bows are broken').

verses.translation_literal: They have plundered him, all who pass by [on] the road; he has become a reproach to his neighbours.
verses.translation_dramatic: And so everyone on the road — everyone passing by — helps themselves. He has become a thing his neighbours sneer at.
verses.directors_commentary:
The walls are down, and the consequences are the picture of a house without a door. 'All who pass by the road' are not armies: they are travellers, merchants, anyone who happens to be going by, and they take what they like. This is the humiliation the singer is dwelling on: the king whose power once made neighbours into vassals, as Radak notes, is now an object of casual theft. Play it with disbelief.

The KJV 'spoil him' is old English for 'rob'; the verb sasah means 'to plunder', and Metzudat Zion links it with 'treading down' (Isa 42:24, 'who gave Jacob to the plunderer'); Metzudat David pictures an abandoned thing that anyone who finds it tramples. The Hebrew has the plural 'they plundered', then 'he has become', singular: the shift from a mob to one humiliated man is the point. 'Reproach' (cherpah) is a word of ancient shaming, the kind that falls on a people who have lost their god's protection. 'Neighbours' (shekhenim) are the nations around Judah.

philological_notes.note: 'They have plundered him': Radak glosses it as 'looted', Metzudat Zion as 'trampled', as in Isaiah 42:24. The verb is used of spoiling a defeated people.
'Reproach': public shame, the mockery of neighbours. Radak notes it reverses the days when the neighbouring kings were subject to David.

verses.translation_literal: You have exalted the right hand of his adversaries; you have made all his enemies rejoice.
verses.translation_dramatic: You have lifted the right hand of those who press him hard. You have given all his enemies reason to sing.
verses.directors_commentary:
In the ancient Near East the right hand is the hand that holds the weapon and strikes, so to 'exalt' it is to give an enemy strength and victory. The verse is built as a deliberate reversal: elsewhere in this psalm it is God's hand that is exalted (verse 14) and the king's enemies that are crushed (verses 22-24). Radak sees exactly this, calling the line the opposite of 'his arm shall strengthen him'. Whoever gives the line should hear the earlier promise under it.

The KJV 'set up' for harimota blurs the key verb: it is rum, 'to raise high', the same root as 'exalted'. 'Adversaries' (tsarav) and 'enemies' ('oyevav) are not synonyms: Malbim distinguishes the tsar, who fights in the field, from the 'oyev, who hates in his heart. The second verb, hismachta, 'made rejoice', is the causative: God is not merely allowing their joy, he is producing it. Ibn Ezra observes that this form of the verb occurs only here.

philological_notes.note: 'The right hand of his adversaries': the sword-hand, the symbol of an enemy's strength. It deliberately reverses the covenant promise that God's right hand is exalted.
'You made rejoice': hiphil, causative. Ibn Ezra notes that this verb form is found only here in Scripture.

verses.translation_literal: Also you turn back the flint of his sword, and you have not raised him up in the battle.
verses.translation_dramatic: You even turn back the keen edge of his sword. And when the fighting came, you did not set him on his feet.
verses.directors_commentary:
The picture now is the battlefield itself. The warrior still has his weapon, but its edge has been blunted and he himself has been left lying where he fell. Let the actor hear the contrast with the king whose throne stood 'before me' like the sun: he is down, and no one stands him up.

The odd word is tsur, here 'flint'. The KJV 'edge' is a sound guess that has the support of Rashi, Radak and Metzudat Zion, who read it as 'sharp edge', pointing to the 'swords of flint' (cherevot tsurim) of Joshua 5:2. Ancient blades were literally flint-edged in Israel's early days, and the word survives for 'sharpness'. The line can also be read as 'you turn back the sword from its rock-hard edge'. 'The battle' with the article is a specific battle, the one that was lost. 'You have not raised him' plays on 'exalted' of the verse before: God lifted the enemy's hand and did not lift the king.

philological_notes.note: 'The flint of his sword': the keen edge. Rashi, Radak and Metzudat Zion all read tsur as 'sharpness', as in 'swords of flint' (Joshua 5:2).
'You have raised him up', 'made him stand': Rashi reads it as 'you did not keep him from falling'; Ibn Ezra 'you did not set him upright after he fell'.

verses.translation_literal: You have made [him] cease from his brightness, and his throne to the ground you have thrown down.
verses.translation_dramatic: You have put out his brightness, the shining that stood about him like noon on a bare hill. And his throne, you have flung it down. It lies on the ground.
verses.directors_commentary: A throne is a king's place in the world, and here it is not toppled by an enemy but thrown by God: the verbs are all "you," the same accusing address that has run since verse 39. Play it as grief with its teeth bared, not as a report. The first word is a hiphil of shabat, "to cease," the verb of the Sabbath, so God is the one who makes the king's days of glory stop. The second word, mitaharo, appears nowhere else in the Bible, and the old readers split on it. Rashi takes it as "his shining," the brightness of midday (the Aramaic tiharah) and the sapphire-clear "purity" of the sky at Exodus 24:10; Meiri and Metzudat Zion agree, with the sense of splendour. Radak reads it as zakhut, "merit," and says it means the kingship that David's house once had. Ibn Ezra goes another way: it is his miqdash, his sanctuary, which is "pure," tied to David's gathering of silver and gold for the Temple. For the stage, brightness serves best: the king's radiance goes out first, then his throne falls. The KJV's "glory" is a safe guess that blurs the light-image and the odd noun; it also smooths "to the ground" into a tidy "cast down to the ground." The Hebrew puts "to the ground" before the verb, so the throne is flung and already lying there when the verb lands. The last verb, migartah, is a rare word for "hurl, bring low." Rashi notes that the Targum Jonathan uses megar for every verb of casting down, and Radak, Meiri and Metzudat Zion all point to the Targum of Genesis 49:17, where "his rider falls backward" becomes "his riders are cast (vimgar) backward." The rider thrown from his mount is the picture: a king hurled, not a king retired.

philological_notes.note: A hapax of uncertain form, with a doubled tet and a hataf-qamets. Most commentators read it as 'his brightness' from the root of 'pure, clear' (compare Exodus 24:10, 'like the very heaven for clearness'). Radak takes it as his merit, his kingship; Ibn Ezra takes it as his pure sanctuary.
'You have hurled down.' Rare in the Hebrew Bible; the Targum uses the same root for casting down. The commentators connect it with Genesis 49:17 in the Targum, where the rider falls backward.

verses.translation_literal: You have made short the days of his youth; you have wrapped shame upon him. Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: You have cut short the days of his youth, and wrapped him in shame like a cloak. Selah.
verses.directors_commentary:
'Youth' ('alumim) is the season of strength and promise, and the verse says it was cut off early. Ibn Ezra and Meiri read this of the dynasty, whose 'young days', its days of rule, did not last; Radak adds that the dynasty's age of shame is long. The speaker is looking at a man, or a house, that should still be in its prime and instead has gone grey in shame.

The KJV 'covered him with shame' is correct in sense, but the verb 'ata is 'to wrap, envelop' (Metzudat Zion: put on, as of a garment, citing Lev 13:45), so the shame is a garment he cannot take off, or a veil over his face (Meiri: so he hides from people). Wear it, do not just hold it. The plural 'alumim, as with 'days', is an abstract of vigour, so 'days of his youth' stays literal. The BBE 'made him old before his time' draws out the sense but loses the image. Selah closes the third movement of the psalm and the actors should pause here before the final plea.

philological_notes.note: 'His youth': the plural of abstraction, 'youthful vigour'. Metzudat Zion compares 'ha'elem' in 1 Samuel 17:56.
'You have wrapped': to cover as with a garment (Metzudat Zion, citing Lev 13:45). Meiri also offers 'veiled', so he hides from the sight of people.

verses.translation_literal: Until when, YHWH, will you hide yourself to perpetuity? Will your anger burn like fire?
verses.translation_dramatic: How long, LORD? How long will you hide? Is it for ever? Will your wrath go on burning like fire?
verses.directors_commentary:
After the accusations the grammar changes: the verbs turn from the finished past ('you have') to the open future ('will you...?'). It is no longer a report but a plea, and the divine name YHWH is spoken here directly, for the first time in this passage. Say it as a question that cannot wait for an answer.

'Until when' (ad mah) is the stock cry of the lament psalms, and the verb 'hide yourself' (tissater) is the usual language for God's face being withdrawn: the opposite of the face that shines, a hiding that leaves the sufferer without protection. 'Burn' (tiv'ar) is the fire of wrath, the same fire that consumes stubble. The KJV 'shall thy wrath burn like fire?' is right, but it joins two questions the Hebrew keeps apart: the first 'until when' governs both clauses, so 'will you hide...? will it burn...?' are one breath (the KJV's 'How long, Lord?' printed here as a standalone question adds a stop the Hebrew lacks). Ibn Ezra reads the line as a double cry: you hide, and yet your wrath burns him, so he is both abandoned and punished.

philological_notes.note: 'Until when?': the standard question of the lament, a shorter form of 'ad matai. Metzudat David takes it as a rhetorical, astonished question.
'Will you hide yourself?': a niphal, reflexive. The hiding is of God's face, which is the withdrawal of help (cf. Radak: as if you do not see the distress of exile).

verses.translation_literal: Remember — I — what [is my] lifespan! For what emptiness have you created all the children of humankind?
verses.translation_dramatic: Remember me — what is my span? What is it worth? Was it for nothing, for breath and emptiness, that you made all the children of Adam?
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker steps back from the king to himself, and then to everyone. The verse is hard to translate because it is clipped: 'Remember — I — what [is] lifespan'. The first word is an imperative to God, and the pronoun 'I' is set in the middle for emphasis, so a good rendering sounds like a man gasping. The actor should lose the polish of the earlier verses.

The KJV 'remember how short my time is' reads the Hebrew mah as exclamatory and resolves the clipped syntax into smooth prose; it is plausible, and the commentators split. Rashi: 'what old age do I have? my days are few'; Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion: chaled is 'a fixed time', the lifespan, which Metzudat Zion links with 'inhabitants of the world' (Ps 49:2, chaled as 'world'). The KJV 'in vain' for shav' flattens a strong word: shav' is emptiness, nothingness, the word for idols and for a false oath. To ask 'for what emptiness?' is to ask whether human life is just nothing. 'Children of humankind' (benei adam) is the whole race, with the pun on adam, 'earth-creature'. The psalm ends its argument with an almost philosophical protest, before the doxology that closes the book.

philological_notes.note: 'Lifespan, duration of life': the same word as 'world' in Psalm 49:2, in the sense of time-bound existence. Metzudat Zion glosses it as 'time'; Ibn Ezra as a fixed, known time.
'Emptiness, nothing': the word used of idols and of falsehood. Rashi glosses it 'for nothing, for futility'.
'Children of humankind': all human beings, which widens the lament from the dynasty to the entire human race.

verses.translation_literal: Who [is the] man [who] will live and not see death, [who] will deliver his life from the hand of Sheol? Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: Who among men will live, and never look on death? Who will pull his own life free from the hand of Sheol? No one. Selah.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm turns here from the king's humiliation to the oldest human fact: everyone dies. The question is rhetorical, and the stage direction is a long silence in which no hand goes up. The Hebrew sets two verbs side by side, "live" and "not see death," and then gives death a grip, a hand: Sheol is a power with a hand that takes hold of a life (nefesh, the whole breathing person, not a detachable soul).

The KJV makes two separate questions and renders שְׁאוֹל as "the grave," which loses that Sheol is the realm of the dead, a place with a hand; Meiri argues from this verse that Sheol can simply mean the grave. The KJV's "soul" is also misleading, since נֶפֶשׁ is a living person, with throat and breath. "Selah" is a musical or liturgical marker of uncertain meaning (a pause, a lifting of voices); in performance, let it be a held silence.

philological_notes.note: Nefesh is the living self, the throat and the breath, not an immortal soul as the English "soul" suggests. "Deliver his life" is more literal than the KJV "soul."
"From the hand of Sheol": Sheol is personified as a power with a hand that seizes. Meiri takes שאול here as the grave, against those who take it as Gehenna everywhere.

verses.translation_literal: Where [are] your former kindnesses, O Lord? You swore to David in your faithfulness.
verses.translation_dramatic: Where are they now, Lord, your first kindnesses, the ones from the beginning? You swore to David. You swore it, and you staked your faithfulness on it.
verses.directors_commentary: The long accusation turns here into a question, and the question is a single word, ayyeh, "where?" It is the cry of someone who remembers a promise and sees nothing. The speaker is not asking for information. He is holding God to what God said. Ancient covenants were sealed by oaths, and a suzerain who swore to a vassal bound himself; so the psalmist is quoting the contract back to its author. Radak says the "kindnesses" are exactly what God swore to David, and asks where they are now that God has abandoned the line. The KJV's "lovingkindnesses" (Coverdale's coinage) is warm but loose: chesed is loyalty inside a bond, the mercy a partner owes because of what was sworn, and the plural here means the acts of that loyalty. The Hebrew has "the former" (harishonim) after the noun, which sets the old days against the present silence. Note also the address: the poet calls him Adonai, "my Lord," a master addressed in submission, where the previous verse spoke to YHWH. The verb nishba'ta is a niphal, the reflexive-passive stem Hebrew uses for swearing, so "you bound yourself by oath" is the force; the KJV's "swarest" is fair. The final "in your faithfulness" (be'emunatekha) is the same word that opened the psalm; it closes a circle with the song of verse 2.

philological_notes.note: The plural of chesed, loyalty owed inside a bond. 'Kindnesses' is too soft; here it means the acts of covenant loyalty that God swore to David.

A niphal of the root of 'oath' (the same consonants as 'seven'), the stem used for swearing: 'you bound yourself by oath'. The oath is the subject of the verse: Radak says the kindnesses are what God swore to David.

verses.translation_literal: Remember, O Lord, the reproach of your servants, my bearing in my bosom all many peoples.
verses.translation_dramatic: Remember, Lord, the taunting of your servants, the scorn of every people, all of it that I carry folded against my chest.
verses.directors_commentary:
A plea to remember, in Hebrew a legal and covenantal act: to "remember" is to act. The speaker moves from "your servants" to "I" and the line becomes physical: the reproach is carried in the bosom (חֵיק), the fold of the robe against the chest where a person carries a child or something precious or heavy. Rashi hears an exile carrying the burden of peoples.

The Hebrew is difficult. "All many peoples" reverses the usual order ("all the many peoples"); Radak, Meiri and Metzudat Zion all read it as "all peoples many," and the KJV supplies "the reproach of" and renders רַבִּים as "mighty," which it does not mean. The KJV also says "how I do bear," turning an infinitive into a clause; the Hebrew is a bare, abrupt "my bearing." The effect is a voice breaking into the first person.

philological_notes.note: "In my bosom": the fold of the garment at the chest, where something is carried close to the body. The reproach is held next to the heart.
Inverted order, read as "all many peoples" by the commentators; the verse has no word for "reproach" after it, so it is understood from the first clause.

verses.translation_literal: Which your enemies have reproached, YHWH, which they have reproached [the] footprints of your anointed.
verses.translation_dramatic: The taunts your enemies have thrown, LORD, the taunts they have thrown at the footsteps of your anointed.
verses.directors_commentary:
Two lines, one word repeated: אֲשֶׁר חֵרְפוּ, "which they have reproached," struck twice like a drum. The first names who is jeering (your enemies, not mine; the speaker makes his shame God's own), the second names the target: the "footprints" (עִקְּבוֹת) of the anointed, the king of David's line. This is the psalm's final turn, from the oath to the king whose crown it was meant to secure.

The KJV's "wherewith… have reproached" is stiff and hides the repetition; and "footsteps" settles an ambiguity. The word comes from עָקֵב, "heel," and the commentators take it as the delay or the trailing end of the king (Radak, Meiri, Metzudat Zion, Ibn Ezra: his steps are late in coming), mocked as never arriving. Rashi reads it as the end of the days of the messianic king. In the plain sense, the enemies are jeering at everything the king does, down to where he sets his heel. Here the YHWH name returns, after אֲדֹנָי in the two verses before.

philological_notes.note: From "heel": footprints, or the heel as the hindmost part of the foot, hence the "delay" or "tail" of the king. The commentators in the packet read it as "the lateness" of the anointed, and Ibn Ezra as "broken heels" that hold up his coming.
"They have reproached": to taunt, to expose to scorn, with the noun חֶרְפָּה of the previous verse as the same root. The repetition of the verb ties both halves of the verse.

verses.translation_literal: Blessed [be] YHWH for ever. Amen and amen.
verses.translation_dramatic: Blessed be the LORD, forever. Amen, and amen.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm ends in the dark and the next line is a blessing. That jolt is not part of the prayer. It is the doxology that closes Book III of the Psalter (Pss 73–89), as similar blessings close Books I, II and IV; the editors set a formula of praise at the end of each book, whatever the mood of the last psalm. The traditional commentaries see two possibilities: the psalmist's own faith breaking through despair (Radak, Meiri), or the scribe closing the book, as copyists still do (Radak and Ibn Ezra both report this).

בָּרוּךְ is a passive participle, "blessed," and carries no verb: the KJV's "Blessed be" is a wish, but the Hebrew could just as well state a fact ("Blessed is the LORD"), as YLT has it. "Amen" (אָמֵן, from the root of "firm, reliable") is a congregational response, "so it is." Said twice, it is a way of saying yes with the whole room; Metzudat David reads the doubling as emphasis. "For ever" is לְעוֹלָם, to the far horizon of time.

philological_notes.note: From the root of "to be firm, reliable," the same root as אֱמוּנָה (v. 50); the people's answer, "so it is." The doubling is for emphasis.
A passive participle with no verb: it can be read as a wish ("may he be blessed") or as a statement ("blessed is"). The closing formula of each book of the Psalter.
